Email Authour Identification¶

Using Enron Email Data Set¶

The Problem¶

Written communication that employs the use of computers is referred to as computer mediated communication (CMC), and email is one of the most important and widely used forms of CMC, especially in the last few decades. Due to its salient features, it is the preferred source of written communication for almost every population connected to the Internet. It is a very quick, asynchronous written communication channel that is used for various purposes ranging from formal to informal communication.

Any illegal act using CMC is termed as a cybercrime. Email is a prime target for cybercriminals, as it has many unique features that enable the facilitation of criminal activity. One can easily hide his/ her identity while sending fraudulent emails, and anonymous messages can be sent to a number of recipients to spread fear among them.

In this Data Tale we are going to build a Classifcation Model using Emails Content from different Authors. Our Classifier will be able recognize patterns in Emails like unique greeting styles or punctuations

Refer to the link for more details on Enron

Data Description¶

The Enron email dataset is a large collection of real emails of an organization, which once was a global organization.

This dataset was collected and prepared by the CALO Project (A Cognitive Assistant that Learns and Organizes). It contains data from about 150 users, mostly senior management of Enron, organized into folders. The corpus contains a total of about 0.5M messages. This data was originally made public, and posted to the web, by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission during its investigation.

The email dataset was later purchased by Leslie Kaelbling at MIT, and turned out to have a number of integrity problems. A number of folks at SRI, notably Melinda Gervasio, worked hard to correct these problems, and it is thanks to them that the dataset is available. The dataset here does not include attachments, and some messages have been deleted "as part of a redaction effort due to requests from affected employees". Invalid email addresses were converted to something of the form user@enron.com whenever possible (i.e., recipient is specified in some parse-able format like "Doe, John" or "Mary K. Smith") and to no_address@enron.com when no recipient was specified.

Credits: Enron

def extract_author(text):
    pattern= r'maildir\\(.*?)\\'
    text= re.findall(pattern, text)
    return text[0]

re.findall(r'maildir/(.*?)/',  'maildir/stclair-c/sent/344.')
Out[17]:
['stclair-c']
We now know the above regex is to extract the email author. Can you tell what it exactly means or what characters set is the target?

This pattern is searching for all the characters in between maildir\\ and \\ .

df['author']= df.file_path.apply(extract_author)

This is what a raw email looks like, lets try and extract different features from this text.

Feature extraction¶

Extracting ID¶

Note that we will be using regex extensively and hence we strongly suggest you to read the regex and try to identify what it translates to in simple english

In [20]:
def find_ID(text):
    pattern= r'Message-ID: \<(.*?)\>'
    text= re.findall(pattern, text)
    return text[0]
df['id']= df.content.apply(find_ID)

This pattern/regex is searching for all the characters between Message-ID: < and >, backshlashes before < and > is to escpae it.

Extracting Date¶

In [21]:
def find_date(text):
    pattern= r'Date: (.*?)\n'
    text= re.findall(pattern, text)
    return text[0]
df['date']= df.content.apply(find_date)

This above regex is also extracting characters between Date: and \n

Rest all the features we will be extracting follows the same pattern.

Extracting Sent From Email-Id¶

In [22]:
def email_from(text):
    pattern= r'From: (.*?)\n'
    text= re.findall(pattern, text)
    return text[0]
df['from_email']= df.content.apply(email_from)

Extracting Sent To Email-Id¶

In [23]:
def email_to(text):
    pattern= r'To: (.*?)\n'
    text= re.findall(pattern, text)
    return text[0]
df['to_email']= df.content.apply(email_to)

Subject¶

In [24]:
def ex_sub(text):
    pattern= r'Subject: (.*?)\n'
    text= re.findall(pattern, text)
    return text[0]
df['subject']= df.content.apply(ex_sub)

Email From Name¶

In [25]:
def name_from(text):
    pattern= r'X-From: (.*?)\n'
    text= re.findall(pattern, text)
    return text[0]
df['from_name']= df.content.apply(name_from)

Email To Name¶

In [26]:
def name_to(text):
    pattern= r'X-To: (.*?)\n'
    text= re.findall(pattern, text)
    return text[0]
df['to_name']= df.content.apply(name_to)

Extracting Content¶

In [27]:
print(df.content[0])

def avg_word_length(row):
    filtered_sentence = ''.join([x for x in row['message'] if x not in '".,;!-'])
    words = filtered_sentence.split()
    try :
        avg = sum(map(len, words)) / len(words)
    except :
        avg = 0
    return avg

def avg_sent_length(row) :
    sents = sent_tokenize(row['message'])
    lengths_of_sents = [len(k) for k in sents]
    avg_length = sum(lengths_of_sents) / len(sents)
    return  avg_length

def ratio_sh_word(row) :
    words= word_tokenize(row['message'])
    sh_words= [word for word in words if len(word) <= 3]
    try:
        ratio_sh =  len(sh_words) / len(words)
        return  ratio_sh
    except Exception:
        return 0

We have seen many features being normalized, why is this important?
Some emails might only have 10 words in turn having lesser punctuations, spaces, digits. However, an email with policy updates will have loads of content also with less punctuations, spaces, digits. When we directly count these attributes, there's a high chance of the computer considering the first email more useful when in reality that might not be the case. To get around this issue we usually divide the attribute with the length of text so we get a percentage of target characters in the text

def get_frequent_punctuation(row):
    punc_dict= {}
    for punc in puncs:
        punc_dict[punc] = row['message'].count(punc)
    return max(punc_dict, key=punc_dict.get)

Text Cleaning¶

This Clean Message function is first substituting everything that is not a chracter with space and then removing the stopwords.

In [102]:
def clean_message(content, remove_stopwords= True):
    content = re.sub("[^a-zA-Z]"," ", content)
    words = word_tokenize(content.lower())
    
    if remove_stopwords:
        stops = set(stopwords.words("english"))
        words = [w for w in words if not w in stops]
    return ' '.join(words)
In [103]:
data.message= data.message.apply(clean_message)

Some algorithms (such as Random Forest classifiers or naive Bayes classifiers) are capable of handling multiple classes directly. Others (such as Support Vector Machine classifiers or Linear classifiers) are strictly binary classifiers.

So now the question is How binary classifiers likes Logistic Regression and Support Vector Machines can classify multiple classes.

There are two approaches to deal with this

  • OneVsOneClassifier
  • OneVsRestClassifier

OneVsRestClassifier

one way to create a system that can classify the Authors Names into 10 classes (from 0 to 9) is to train 10 binary classifiers, one for each Author (a 0-detector, a 1-detector, a 2-detector, and so on). Then when you want to classify an image, you get the decision score from each classifier for that image and you select the class whose classifier outputs the highest score.

OneVsOneClassifier

Another strategy is to train a binary classifier for every pair of Authors: one to distinguish 0s and 1s, another to distinguish 0s and 2s, another for 1s and 2s, and so on. This is called the one-versus-one (OvO) strategy.So, If there are N classes, you need to train N × (N – 1) / 2 classifiers.

Scikit-Learn detects when you try to use a binary classifier algorithm for a multi-class classification task, and it automatically runs OneVsRestClassifier or OneVsOneClassifier, depending on the algorithm.

Now we have a problem here for some authors the classifier is working perfect but for other the classifier is under performing. So accuracy won't be great measure.

For a binary classification task we know these metrics

But What if you are dealing with multiple classes in our example we have 10 Classes

Here we need to macro and micro averaging of your classification metrics

Micro Average

Macro Average

And the same goes for Recall and F1 Score.

So Now Another question When to use Micro and when to use Micro!!

Macro-average method can be used when you want to know how the system performs overall across the sets of data.

On the other hand, micro-average can be a useful measure when your dataset varies in size.

We will use macro average F1 Score as our evaluation metrics.

In [122]:
print(f1_score(y_pred, y_test, average= 'macro'))

Conclusion:¶

The major part in our classification problem is to find and create features to provide as much information as possible. That being said, all algorithms might not perform well and hence it is necessary for us to try using different algorithms. For now we have a 91.89% accuracy overall with a Logistic regression model. There is a great chance to improve model performance by tuning, using advanced models. This notebook is not intended to give a solution but to walk you through the process. So we encourage you to go ahead and improve upon the existing progress
